card.keepWhy: Don’t ask who counts. Be the neighbor.
sources: John 4:9 (“Jews have no dealings with Samaritans”), behind shot 4
Luke 10:25-28 (a lawyer tests Jesus; love God with all your heart and your neighbor as yourself, from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18)
Luke 10:29 (“But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, ‘Who is my neighbor?’”)
Luke 10:30 (a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers, who left him half dead)
Luke 10:31-32 (a priest and a Levite pass by on the other side)

Luke 10:33-35 (a Samaritan is moved with compassion, bandages his wounds pouring on oil and wine, brings him to an inn, pays two denarii: “Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return”)
Luke 10:36-37 (“Which of these three seems to you to have been a neighbor?” “He who showed mercy on him.” “Go and do likewise”)
Mark 4:33-34 (Jesus taught the crowds with many parables, as they were able to hear), behind the teach step
Captions follow the World English Bible, lightly modernized
check: The script’s day 22 topic is “why he told stories” (Mark 4:33-34); this lesson carries it through the Good Samaritan, where Jesus answers a question with a story. Confirm the fit.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? ever walked past someone who needed help, and thought about it all day?
options: me too. that feeling is worth listening to. so is this story.
that’s a gift. this story is about people like you.
good. keep this one for the next time.

steps.line: A lawyer agreed the great law was to love God and love your neighbor. Then, to test Jesus, he asked, “And who is my neighbor?”
steps.label: Luke 10:25-29

steps.line: Jesus didn’t give a definition. He told a story. A man was going down the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, and robbers left him half dead.
steps.label: Luke 10:30

steps.line: A priest came by, saw him, and passed by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple helper, did the same.
steps.label: Luke 10:31-32

steps.q: A priest, then a Levite, have passed by. Who do you guess stops next?
steps.why: Listeners expected the trio priest, Levite, Israelite: an ordinary local would be the hero. Jesus swaps in a Samaritan, the last one they’d pick.

steps.line: Then a Samaritan, from a people many listeners mistrusted, saw him and was moved with compassion. He bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine.
steps.label: Luke 10:33-34

steps.q: Why might Jesus make the hero a Samaritan, not someone his listeners admired?
o: Because Samaritans were known as healers
To embarrass the lawyer in public
To show love crosses every line people draw
steps.why: Jews and Samaritans had feuded for centuries over where God should be worshipped; John’s Gospel says they had no dealings with each other (4:9). The man the listeners would least expect is the one who loves.

steps.line: He took him to an inn and paid for his care. “Look after him. Whatever more you spend, I’ll repay you when I return.”
steps.label: Luke 10:34-35

steps.q: Jesus asks, “Which of these three was a neighbor?” What do you guess the lawyer answers?
steps.why: He can’t quite bring himself to say “Samaritan.” Many readers hear that dodge as the story’s sharpest moment.

steps.line: “Which of these three was a neighbor to the man?” “The one who showed mercy.” Jesus said, “Go and do the same.”
steps.label: Luke 10:36-37

steps.q: Why would Jesus’s listeners nod at “the road down to Jericho”?
o: It was steep, lonely, known for robbers
It was a new Roman road, safe and busy
steps.why: It drops about 1,000 meters (over 3,000 feet) in under 20 miles of desert. Everyone knew it was a place you could get jumped.

say: here’s what i love. jesus could have given a lecture. instead he told a story, and let the lawyer answer his own question.
the gospels say he taught the crowds in stories, as much as they could hear. christians read this one as a call: don’t ask who counts as your neighbor. be one.

steps.q: Some readers defend the priest: the man looked half dead. Why might that matter to a priest?
o: Priests weren’t meant to travel alone
Touching a corpse made a priest unclean
Only Levites were supposed to help
steps.why: Leviticus 21:1 keeps priests away from the dead. Others point out he was heading away from Jerusalem, so the excuse is thin. Jesus doesn’t argue the rule; he just shows who stopped.

today.say: notice one person today you’d usually walk past, a coworker, a neighbor, someone on the street, and stop for them: a hello, a hand, a coffee. that’s “go and do the same.”
options: good. they’re usually closer than you think.
then you already know which road to take today.
